nameStory: This microscopic plant doesn't have a common name because it's so tiny that most people never notice it! The scientific name Staurodesmus comes from Greek words meaning "cross-shaped chain," referring to how these single-celled algae often link together in star-like patterns. The species name "cuspidatus" means "pointed," describing the sharp spines that stick out from each cell.
description: Staurodesmus cuspidatus is a microscopic single-celled green alga that you'd need a magnifying glass or microscope to see clearly. Each cell is shaped like a tiny green gem with pointed spines sticking out, and they're often found floating in quiet freshwater or forming delicate chains. Individual cells are incredibly small - less than the width of a human hair. This is actually a plant, not an animal, and it makes its own food through photosynthesis like larger green plants do.

idTips.label: Cell shape and spines
idTips.description: Under magnification, cells appear gem-like or diamond-shaped with 2-4 sharp, pointed spines extending outward - these spines are the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Cells have a vivid emerald green color due to chlorophyll, making them stand out against clear water when viewed through a lens

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Extremely tiny - individual cells are typically 15-30 micrometers wide (much smaller than the period at the end of this sentence)

idTips.label: Chain formation
idTips.description: Often found linked together in short chains or clusters, creating delicate star-like patterns visible under magnification

idTips.label: Cell wall texture
idTips.description: Cell walls appear smooth and glassy under magnification, with a crisp, defined outline that looks almost crystal-like

habitat: Found in clean, quiet freshwater environments throughout New England, including ponds, slow-moving streams, and the shallow edges of lakes. Prefers slightly acidic to neutral water and is often found among other microscopic algae in areas with good water quality. Most commonly discovered in woodland ponds and beaver ponds where the water is still and nutrient-rich but not polluted.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm, often becoming noticeable in late spring when other aquatic life becomes active.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when cells are most abundant and active, reproducing rapidly in warm water with long daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though some may persist in warmer microhabitats.
seasonality.winter: Dormant or present in very low numbers, with some cells surviving under ice in protected pond environments.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny organisms are master architects - they can split perfectly in half to reproduce, with each half rebuilding its missing spines and cell wall in a matter of hours, like biological 3D printing!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spiny desmid algae, but Staurodesmus has fewer, more prominent spines compared to its relatives. Remember: "Stauro-SPINES" - look for the distinctive pointed projections that are fewer but more dramatic than other similar species.
contextualKnowledge: Though called an "alga," this organism is actually classified as a plant and plays the same ecological role as larger plants, producing oxygen and forming the base of aquatic food webs. Many people don't realize that some of our most important plants are microscopic and that you need magnification to see much of the botanical diversity around us.
compareHints: Staurodesmus cuspidatus has more prominent, sharper spines than most of its relatives in the genus. While S. triangularis has a more triangular overall shape, and S. glaber lacks spines entirely, S. cuspidatus is distinguished by having 2-4 very pronounced, pointed spines that extend clearly from the cell body. Among desmid algae generally, Staurodesmus species are recognized by their spiny, angular appearance compared to the smooth, crescent shapes of Closterium species.
